title: 10 Paid PhD Positions at University of Marburg 2027: Doctoral Research on Gender and International Criminal Law in Germany
summary: The University of Marburg in Germany is accepting applications for ten Doctoral Researcher/PhD positions within the new DFG Research Training Group 3159, “Gender and Gendering in Contexts of International Criminal Law.” Hosted by the International Centre for War Crimes Trials (ICWC) at the University of Marburg, the Research Training Group brings together scholars from multiple disciplines to investigate how gender and processes of gendering interact with international criminal law, transitional justice, institutions, societies, and the broader conditions under which international criminal justice operates. The positions offer selected doctoral researchers the opportunity to complete an independent PhD project in an international, interdisciplinary, and structured research environment while being employed by the University of Marburg. A total of 10 positions are available. Successful applicants are expected to begin on 1 February 2027 . The positions are offered for up to four years, with contracts running until 31 January 2031 , subject to applicable German academic employment regulations. The positions are 75% part-time appointments and are remunerated according to TV-H pay grade E13 at 75% , the public-sector salary framework used in the German state of Hesse. Applications must be submitted by 4 October 2026 . About the University of Marburg The University of Marburg, formally known as Philipps-Universität Marburg , was founded in 1527 and is one of Germany s historic universities. Today, the institution serves approximately 22,000 students and conducts research across a broad range of academic disciplines. The advertised doctoral positions are based within the University s International Centre for War Crimes Trials , an interdisciplinary institution focusing on international criminal law, transitional justice, accountability, war crimes, and related political, historical, legal, and societal questions. The doctoral researchers will form part of DFG Research Training Group 3159 , creating a structured environment in which PhD candidates can develop individual dissertation projects while participating in a wider collaborative research programme. About DFG Research Training Group 3159 The Research Training Group is titled: Gender and Gendering in Contexts of International Criminal Law Its central research focus concerns the complex relationships between concepts of gender and international criminal law. Rather than examining international criminal law exclusively as a technical legal system, the programme investigates the wider legal, political, institutional, cultural, social, and historical contexts in which international criminal justice operates. The Research Training Group asks how: Gender shapes international criminal law; Processes of gendering influence international criminal justice; International criminal law itself constructs or reproduces ideas about gender; Gender influences institutions responsible for criminal accountability; Gender affects how crimes are understood, categorized, prosecuted, or remembered; International criminal law interacts with social and political structures; Gender shapes the application, function, and impact of international criminal justice. The programme is intentionally interdisciplinary. This means doctoral candidates are not restricted to legal research. Applicants from social sciences, humanities, law, economics, theology, and related fields are encouraged to develop projects that contribute to the Research Training Group s overarching questions. Number of PhD Positions Available The University of Marburg is recruiting: 10 Doctoral Researchers/PhD candidates for the Research Training Group. This cohort-based structure gives selected doctoral researchers the opportunity to develop their own dissertations alongside other researchers working on connected questions. The programme therefore combines: Independent doctoral research; Structured supervision; Interdisciplinary exchange; Collaborative research; International academic engagement; Professional development. Starting Date The positions are scheduled to begin on: 1 February 2027 Applicants should therefore be available to commence their doctoral employment and research programme around this date. Contract Duration The positions are offered until: 31 January 2031 This corresponds to a maximum period of approximately four years. However, the announcement notes that previous periods of academic qualification employment may need to be taken into consideration under German academic employment law. The employment limitation is governed by Section 2(1) of the German Academic Fixed-Term Contract Act , commonly known as the Wissenschaftszeitvertragsgesetz or WissZeitVG . The contract period is intended to provide sufficient time for candidates to undertake the scientific research necessary to complete their doctoral qualifications. Salary and Employment Conditions Successful candidates will be employed under the public-sector salary framework of the German state of Hesse. The position is classified as: TV-H E13, 75% The employment volume is therefore: 75% of regular working hours Applicants should understand that this is a salaried doctoral researcher position , rather than a conventional scholarship that simply provides a stipend. Candidates will be employees of the University and will combine doctoral research with responsibilities associated with the Research Training Group. Main Responsibilities The doctoral researchers will have three principal responsibilities. 1. Complete a Doctoral Degree The primary purpose of the position is to undertake an independent doctoral research project. The dissertation topic must fall within the broader research programme of RTG 3159. Applicants are therefore expected to develop an original research question that connects meaningfully with themes concerning: Gender; Gendering; International criminal law; Transitional justice; International criminal justice; Related institutional, legal, political, historical, economic, cultural, religious, or societal questions. The exact topic will depend on the applicant s disciplinary background and research interests. 2. Provide Research Assistance within the Research Training Group Doctoral researchers will also contribute research assistance to the broader research programme of the RTG. This reflects the collaborative nature of a DFG Research Training Group. Candidates should therefore be willing to contribute not only to their individual dissertation but also to the intellectual development of the wider programme. 3. Participate Actively in RTG Activities Successful candidates must actively participate in the Research Training Group s activities. Importantly, on-site participation in the RTG s core programme is mandatory . Applicants should therefore not regard the positions as remote PhDs. While individual research may involve travel, fieldwork, archives, conferences, or international collaboration, doctoral researchers are expected to be physically present for the programme s central academic activities in Marburg. Academic Background Required Applicants must hold an above-average completed university degree equivalent to a: Master s degree; State examination; or Comparable higher university qualification. The degree should be in a discipline relevant to the Research Training Group. The announcement particularly identifies the following fields. Peace and Conflict Studies Candidates from peace and conflict studies may develop projects examining areas such as: Transitional justice; Conflict-related violence; Post-conflict accountability; Gender and peacebuilding; International criminal justice; Conflict transformation. Gender Studies Gender studies is directly relevant to the programme s core intellectual agenda. Potential research could engage with questions involving: Gender theory; Feminist theory; Masculinities; Queer theory; Intersectionality; Gendered institutions; Gendered forms of violence; Gender and justice. History Historians may approach international criminal justice and gender from historical perspectives. Possible research areas could include the development of international criminal institutions, historical war-crimes trials, changing legal concepts, memory, or gendered understandings of conflict and accountability. Modern German Literature The programme also explicitly welcomes relevant applicants from modern German literary studies. Potential projects may engage with representation, discourse, memory, law, gender, violence, testimony, or cultural responses to international crimes. Political Science Political scientists may investigate topics related to: International institutions; Global governance; Transitional justice; Conflict; Gender politics; International organizations; Accountability; International criminal courts; Politics of prosecution. Law Applicants from law may be particularly well placed to examine doctrinal and theoretical questions surrounding: International criminal law; International humanitarian law; Human rights law; Gender-based crimes; Sexual violence; International tribunals; Transitional justice. Sociology Sociological projects may explore how international criminal justice interacts with: Social structures; Institutions; Communities; Gender norms; Identities; Power relations; Collective memory; Social change. Theology Theology is also identified as a relevant discipline, reflecting the programme s broad interdisciplinary approach. Possible areas might include religion, gender, conflict, reconciliation, ethics, justice, memory, or post-conflict societies. Economics Applicants with an economics background may also be eligible where their proposed project connects convincingly with the RTG s research agenda. The list of disciplines is introduced as particularly relevant rather than necessarily exhaustive. Applicants from related fields should therefore assess whether their academic training and proposed project fit the Research Training Group s central research questions. Previous Research Knowledge Prior knowledge of the Research Training Group s main subject areas is considered advantageous. Relevant background may include experience with: International law; International criminal law; Transitional justice; Gender studies. This knowledge is described as an advantage rather than an absolute standalone eligibility requirement. Applicants from adjacent disciplines may therefore still be competitive if they can demonstrate a convincing intellectual connection between their existing background and their proposed doctoral research. English Language Requirement Applicants must demonstrate English proficiency of at least: C1 level according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages Proof of English-language proficiency must be included in the application. Because the programme is international and interdisciplinary, candidates should be capable of: Academic reading; Academic writing; Research presentations; Seminar participation; Interdisciplinary discussion; Professional communication at an advanced level in English. Is German Required? German-language proficiency is not presented as an absolute prerequisite . However, German skills are considered an advantage. Candidates who do not currently speak German should demonstrate a: Willingness to learn German. This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to international applicants who already possess strong English-language skills but may not yet have advanced German proficiency. Personal and Professional Qualities In addition to academic qualifications, candidates should demonstrate: Team spirit; Strong commitment to academic excellence; Interest in interdisciplinary research; Willingness to collaborate; Capacity for independent scientific research; Commitment to completing a doctoral qualification. The programme is designed for researchers who can work independently while contributing actively to a collaborative academic community. Interdisciplinary Research Is Central One of the most important characteristics of RTG 3159 is its interdisciplinary structure. Applicants should therefore avoid developing a dissertation proposal that is intellectually isolated from the wider programme. The proposed research should be suitable for dialogue with scholars from other disciplines. For example, a legal research project may benefit from considering: Political institutions; Historical developments; Gender theory; Social structures; Cultural narratives. Similarly, a sociology, political science, history, or gender-studies project should demonstrate a meaningful relationship with international criminal law or the broader systems surrounding it. Structured Doctoral Supervision Successful candidates will receive structured doctoral supervision. Each doctoral researcher will have an individually composed: Thesis Advisory Committee This committee is intended to provide structured guidance throughout the doctoral project. Such supervision can help candidates with: Research design; Dissertation planning; Academic development; Research challenges; Publication strategies; Career planning; Interdisciplinary integration. Individual Qualification and Supervision Programme The Research Training Group will provide an individual qualification programme tailored to both: The doctoral researcher; and The individual dissertation project. This provides an opportunity for candidates to develop not only their thesis but also a broader academic research profile. International and Interdisciplinary Research Environment The University emphasizes that the successful doctoral researchers will join an: Inspiring; International; Interdisciplinary academic environment. A major objective of the programme is to enable doctoral candidates to build their own independent research profiles . This can be particularly useful for candidates considering longer-term careers in: Academia; International organizations; Transitional justice; Human rights; Policy research; International criminal justice; NGOs; Research institutes; Legal institutions. Additional University Support Doctoral researchers will also have access to support and professional-development structures within the University of Marburg. These include support from: Marburg University Research Academy The Research Academy provides doctoral and early-career researchers with training and professional-development opportunities. International Office International doctoral researchers can receive institutional support related to international mobility and integration. Family Service The University describes itself as family-friendly and provides services intended to help employees balance professional and family responsibilities. Higher Education Didactics Candidates can also access university services related to higher education teaching and pedagogical development. Research Environment and Inclusion The University describes the research environment as: Collegial; Family-friendly; LGBTIQ+-inclusive. The University also explicitly encourages applications from women. In areas where women are underrepresented, female candidates may be preferred when applicants have equal qualifications. Applicants with disabilities, as defined under the relevant provisions of Germany s Social Security Code, may also receive preference in cases of equal qualifications. Application Documents Applications may be submitted in: German or English Candidates must prepare several substantial documents. 1. Doctoral Project Outline Applicants must submit an outline of their planned doctoral research project. Maximum length: 10 pages The page limit includes: Research proposal; Work schedule; Time schedule; Bibliography. The proposal must be based on an: Innovative research question that aligns with the topic and research programme of RTG 3159. The project should also be suitable for interdisciplinary collaboration. This is likely to be one of the most important components of the application. What Should the Doctoral Proposal Demonstrate? Although the announcement does not prescribe a detailed proposal template, the research outline should clearly demonstrate: The proposed research problem; Central research question; Relevance to gender and gendering; Connection with international criminal law; Original academic contribution; Theoretical framework; Methodological approach; Interdisciplinary relevance; Feasibility within the four-year period; Planned research stages. Candidates should ensure that their proposal connects explicitly to the Research Training Group rather than simply submitting a generic PhD proposal. 2. Writing Sample Applicants must submit a writing sample of no more than: 25 pages Possible writing samples include: Sections from a Master s thesis; Table of contents and selected Master s thesis chapters; Seminar paper; Research paper; Academic article; Blog entry. The writing sample allows the selection committee to assess the applicant s research, analytical, and writing abilities. Candidates should ideally choose work that demonstrates qualities relevant to the proposed PhD. 3. Motivation Letter Applicants must submit a letter explaining their motivation. A strong motivation letter should connect: Previous academic background; Research interests; Proposed doctoral project; Interest in RTG 3159; Interest in interdisciplinary research; Career goals. Rather than simply describing the University as prestigious, applicants should explain why this specific Research Training Group is a strong intellectual fit. 4. Curriculum Vitae A current CV is required. Candidates should include relevant: Academic qualifications; Research experience; Employment; Publications; Conference participation; Research projects; Teaching; Academic service; Language abilities; Awards. 5. Certificates of Qualification Applicants must submit certificates documenting their completed qualifications. This includes evidence of the university degree that qualifies them for doctoral research. 6. Evidence of Academic Activities Where applicable, candidates should include documentation of relevant academic activities. These might include research, publications, conference contributions, academic employment, or other scholarly work. 7. Transcript of Records A complete academic transcript must be submitted. The transcript should document courses and academic performance from the applicant s relevant degree programme. 8. Proof of English Proficiency Applicants must provide evidence demonstrating English proficiency at: C1 level or higher Candidates should review the application system carefully to determine which forms of certification are accepted. 9. Academic Recommendation or Master s Thesis Evaluation Applicants must provide one of the following: One academic letter of recommendation , OR The first examiner s report/evaluation of the Master s thesis This flexibility is important for candidates who may find it easier to provide an official Master s thesis examiner report than request a separate reference. Application Checklist Before submitting, applicants should ensure they have: Doctoral project outline, maximum 10 pages; Work and time schedule included in the proposal; Bibliography included within the 10-page limit; Writing sample, maximum 25 pages; Motivation letter; CV; Qualification certificates; Evidence of academic activities where applicable; Transcript of records; Proof of English C1 proficiency; One academic recommendation OR first examiner s Master s thesis report. Selection Interviews Digital interviews are expected to take place from: Late October to early November 2026 Applicants shortlisted after the document review should therefore monitor their email closely during this period and be prepared for an online interview. Candidates may reasonably expect the interview to explore their proposed research, disciplinary background, motivation, interdisciplinary fit, and suitability for the Research Training Group. Application Deadline The final deadline is: 4 October 2026 Applicants should submit their complete application by this date. Given that the research proposal alone can be up to 10 pages and requires an innovative project aligned with the RTG research programme, prospective candidates should begin preparing significantly before October. Important Dates Applications: Open Application deadline: 4 October 2026 Expected interviews: Late October to early November 2026 Employment and PhD start: 1 February 2027 Contract end: 31 January 2031 Maximum duration: Approximately four years Registration Number Applicants should note the official vacancy registration number: ZE-0063-ICWC-wmz-2026 This reference may be useful when communicating with the University about the vacancy. Contact for Further Information Questions concerning the doctoral positions or Research Training Group may be directed to: Prof. Dr. Stefanie Bock Telephone: +49 6421-28 23119 Email: rtg3159@uni-marburg.de Further information about the Research Training Group is available HERE . Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application Start With the Research Training Group, Not Just Your Existing Interests Read the RTG research programme carefully before finalizing your proposal. A strong application should demonstrate that the candidate understands what the programme is trying to investigate. Make Gender Central to the Research Question The programme is specifically concerned with gender and gendering. Gender should therefore be analytically important to the project rather than appearing only as a secondary variable added to an otherwise unrelated proposal. Establish a Strong Connection to International Criminal Law Applicants from non-law disciplines should explain clearly how their project interacts with international criminal justice. This connection could be: Institutional; Political; Historical; Sociological; Cultural; Economic; Religious; Legal. Demonstrate Interdisciplinary Potential The application should show how the project could benefit from conversations with researchers outside the applicant s own field. Develop a Realistic Four-Year Timeline Candidates should show that the proposed research can reasonably be completed within the employment period. The time plan should account for major stages such as: Literature review; Theoretical development; Data gathering where applicable; Archival or field research; Analysis; Chapter writing; Revision; Dissertation submission. Choose Your Writing Sample Carefully The strongest writing sample is not necessarily the longest or most prestigious piece. Choose work that best demonstrates: Independent thinking; Clear argumentation; Research ability; Methodological competence; Academic writing. Explain Why Marburg and RTG 3159 Your motivation letter should make clear why this programme provides a particularly strong environment for your project. Specificity is more persuasive than generic praise. Conclusion The 10 Doctoral Researcher/PhD positions at the University of Marburg s DFG Research Training Group 3159 offer a substantial opportunity for emerging researchers interested in the intersections of gender, gendering, international criminal law, transitional justice, conflict, institutions, society, and accountability . Successful applicants will join an international and interdisciplinary doctoral cohort at the International Centre for War Crimes Trials and receive structured supervision through an individually composed Thesis Advisory Committee. The appointments run for up to four years, beginning 1 February 2027 and ending 31 January 2031 , and are paid according to TV-H E13 at 75% employment . The programme welcomes applicants from a broad range of relevant disciplines, including peace and conflict studies, gender studies, history, modern German literature, political science, law, sociology, theology, and economics. Applicants need an above-average relevant university degree, at least C1-level English, a strong research profile, and an original doctoral project aligned with the RTG s interdisciplinary research agenda. German is advantageous but applicants who are willing to learn German may also be considered. The application requires a substantial doctoral proposal, writing sample, motivation letter, academic records, proof of English proficiency, and either an academic recommendation or the first examiner s report on the applicant s Master s thesis. The application deadline is 4 October 2026 , with online selection interviews expected from late October through early November. For researchers seeking a salaried PhD position combining international criminal justice with gender-focused interdisciplinary research, this opportunity provides a particularly structured pathway to developing an independent academic profile in Germany. For further information about this opportunity, VISIT HERE . For more doctoral, research, and international opportunities, visit www.opportunitiesforyouth.org . title: Melton Foundation 2027 Applications Open: Global Solvers Accelerator and Global Citizenship Learning Program for Young Changemakers
summary: Applications are now open for two major Melton Foundation opportunities for 2027: the Global Solvers Accelerator and the Global Citizenship Learning Program. Both programs are designed to develop globally minded leaders, strengthen community impact and connect emerging changemakers with an international network committed to sustainable development and global citizenship. Although both opportunities provide pathways into the Melton Foundation’s lifelong global community, they serve different applicants. The Global Solvers Accelerator is intended for young social-impact practitioners who are already leading or actively involved in a community project. The Global Citizenship Learning Program is designed specifically for university students enrolled at one of the Melton Foundation’s five partner institutions. Applications for both 2027 cohorts opened on 15 August 2026 and will close on 15 November 2026. Prospective applicants should carefully compare the eligibility requirements before selecting the most appropriate program. Melton Foundation 2027 Programs at a Glance Detail Global Solvers Accelerator Global Citizenship Learning Program Target participants Young social-impact and community-development practitioners University students interested in community impact and global citizenship Age requirement 20–35 years 18–25 years Geographic scope Open to eligible applicants worldwide Restricted to students at five partner universities Existing project required Yes No established track record is required Main format Virtual learning with a fully funded in-person Co-Lab Virtual learning with a fully sponsored Global Citizens’ Connect Learning period Eight-month core program, supported by onboarding and transition activities Ten-month program from March to December 2027 Weekly commitment Approximately four hours Approximately three to four hours Program cost USD 900 if selected; partial need-based support is available No program fee Application deadline 15 November 2026 15 November 2026 Long-term outcome Entry into the Melton Fellowship after successful completion Entry into the Melton Fellowship after successful completion About the Melton Foundation The Melton Foundation is an international organization focused on developing people who can collaborate across cultures, identities, sectors and geographic boundaries. Its programs connect local community action with global citizenship and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Rather than offering isolated training events, the Foundation develops sustained learning communities. Participants are expected to contribute actively, learn from people with different experiences and apply their learning to practical social or community challenges. Successful participants in both programs can eventually join the Melton Fellowship, a lifelong international community offering continued opportunities for mentoring, collaboration, leadership development, learning and social-impact partnerships. Opportunity One: Global Solvers Accelerator 2027 What Is the Global Solvers Accelerator? The Global Solvers Accelerator is a leadership, project-development and peer-learning program for emerging changemakers between 20 and 35 years of age. It brings together approximately 15 to 20 practitioners from different countries who are already working on community-based or social-impact initiatives. Participants use the program to examine their leadership practices, address unresolved project challenges, learn from international peers and improve the effectiveness and sustainability of their initiatives. The Accelerator is not simply a business-growth program. Its emphasis is on reflective leadership, shared learning, collaborative problem-solving and the development of stronger social-impact projects. Participants bring actual problems, decisions and operational challenges from their initiatives into a structured international learning environment. Previous participants have worked in areas including: Education and learning equity Climate action and environmental sustainability Public health Civic engagement Community livelihoods Disability inclusion Human rights Social equity Youth empowerment Technology for social good Other areas connected with sustainable development Global Solvers Accelerator Learning Structure The core Accelerator runs from 1 April to 30 November 2027 and includes eight interconnected learning modules. Selected participants are expected to complete onboarding activities in March 2027 before entering the main learning phase. The program combines: Facilitated thematic modules Bi-weekly virtual sessions Independent assignments and preparation Peer-to-peer learning Project-based exercises Practical social-impact tools Subject-matter advice Mentoring and personalized support Cross-cultural dialogue Collaborative problem-solving Reflection on leadership, systems and project strategy According to the official GSA frequently asked questions , learning topics may include project effectiveness, team dynamics, collective leadership, intersectionality, social innovation, regenerative practices, impact modelling, systems-based approaches, strategic visibility, audience engagement, and monitoring and evaluation. Participants also map their projects against the Sustainable Development Goals. The purpose is not to limit projects to selected SDGs, but to help participants understand how their local initiatives connect with the wider, interconnected sustainable-development agenda. Levels of Impact The Accelerator is designed to produce change at three interconnected levels: Individual development Participants strengthen their leadership capacity, intercultural understanding, critical reflection and ability to work across differences. Community-level impact Participants apply new methods, ideas and relationships to strengthen the projects they are implementing in their respective communities. Wider systemic impact By exchanging locally grounded knowledge across countries and sectors, participants can identify common challenges, adapt successful approaches and contribute to wider progress toward sustainable development. Who Should Apply? The Global Solvers Accelerator is suitable for applicants who: Are between 20 and 35 years old. Are actively involved in or leading a community or social-impact project. Can demonstrate a genuine commitment to creating positive change. Are interested in improving their leadership and project practices. Are willing to learn through peer exchange and honest reflection. Can collaborate respectfully with people from different cultures and backgrounds. Have sufficient English-language ability to participate in all program activities. Can commit approximately four hours per week. Can participate in virtual sessions and complete independent assignments. Can maintain at least a 75% participation rate. An academic degree or a particular field of study is not identified as a mandatory requirement. However, having an existing social-impact project or initiative is essential. Project Eligibility Requirements Applicants cannot apply without a project. The initiative may be at an early planning stage or already under implementation, but it must: Already exist as a concrete project or documented project plan. Address a real community or social challenge. Be connected to a particular community, territory or on-the-ground context. Continue for at least the duration of the Accelerator. Provide the applicant with sufficient responsibility or involvement to apply the program’s learning. Applications are submitted by individuals rather than project teams. If several people are working on one initiative, the group should nominate the member best positioned to represent the project and apply. Global Solvers Co-Lab 2027 Actively engaged participants will be invited to the Global Solvers Co-Lab, the Accelerator’s fully funded, week-long in-person component. The 2027 Co-Lab is tentatively scheduled for 19–26 July 2027. It is designed as an intensive working experience where participants meet their peers, examine projects, exchange practical knowledge, develop collaborations and design new approaches to community impact. Applicants should understand that the Co-Lab is not a sightseeing trip or leisure retreat. Participants should expect structured activities, collaborative workshops, shared learning environments and an intensive schedule. Benefits of the Global Solvers Accelerator Selected participants can expect to: Improve their leadership and decision-making capacity. Receive structured support for an existing social-impact project. Learn practical tools for project planning, implementation and evaluation. Strengthen their understanding of systems, communities and sustainable development. Obtain constructive feedback from international peers. Build relationships with social-impact practitioners from different countries. Access mentoring and subject-matter guidance. Develop approaches to project communication and strategic visibility. Participate in a fully funded international Co-Lab, subject to active engagement. Join the Melton Foundation’s lifelong community after successful completion. The Foundation reports that, among its 2025 Accelerator participants, 94% became more intentional about collaboration and partnerships, while 91% reported a strong sense of trust and belonging within the community. Program Fee and Financial Support The program fee for the 2027 Global Solvers Accelerator is USD 900, payable only after an applicant has been selected. Need-based financial support is available at different levels, covering 20%, 50% or up to 80% of the fee. Full fee support is not currently offered. Applicants receiving the maximum 80% support would remain responsible for 20% of the program fee. Requesting financial support does not negatively affect the selection decision. However, applicants must request it in their original application. Requests submitted after the application stage cannot be considered. Applicants seeking financial support must generally prepare: A personal statement explaining their financial circumstances and need for assistance. An endorsement letter from a credible reference, such as a project supervisor or co-leader. Applicants should consult the official GSA Application Guide for the exact documentation requirements. Global Solvers Accelerator Application and Selection Timeline The anticipated process is: Application period: 15 August–15 November 2026 Application and reference review: December 2026–January 2027 Virtual Assessment Centre: tentatively around 30–31 January 2027 Onboarding: March 2027 Core Accelerator: 1 April–30 November 2027 Global Solvers Co-Lab: tentatively 19–26 July 2027 Transition into the Melton Fellowship: after successful program completion The official main page and FAQ currently display different tentative Assessment Centre dates—30 and 31 January 2027—so shortlisted applicants should follow the date stated in their invitation. Applicants may submit the Global Solvers Accelerator 2027 application here . Opportunity Two: Global Citizenship Learning Program 2027 What Is the Global Citizenship Learning Program? The Global Citizenship Learning Program is a ten-month learning and leadership experience for university students who want to understand global challenges, collaborate across cultures and create positive change in their communities. The program runs online from March to December 2027 and combines eight learning modules with onboarding, practical assignments, intercultural dialogue, community-impact work and a transition into the lifelong Melton Fellowship. Unlike the Global Solvers Accelerator, applicants are not required to have an established social-impact initiative or an extensive record of leadership. The selection process places considerable emphasis on motivation, potential, curiosity and commitment to community impact. What Participants Will Learn Participants develop practical and interpersonal competencies such as: Intercultural awareness and communication Critical thinking Empathy and active listening Inclusive and ethical leadership Project management Systems thinking Storytelling Collaborative problem-solving Teamwork across cultures Understanding inequality, privilege and inclusion Connecting global challenges with local realities Sustainable Development Goal implementation Students work with international peers, Senior Melton Fellows and community partners to co-create projects aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals. These are intended to produce real community outcomes rather than remain theoretical classroom exercises. Program Format and Time Commitment The program involves approximately three to four hours of participation per week, equivalent to around 12 to 16 hours per month. A typical month may include: Self-paced learning materials Two live virtual cohort meetings Progress on a community-impact project Campus or local-team meetings Required readings and preparatory activities Group discussions Collaborative assignments Reflection and peer-learning exercises Live sessions are generally held twice monthly, commonly on the first and third Saturdays. Participants must also have access to a laptop or desktop computer, stable internet, a camera and a microphone. Who Can Apply? Applicants must: Be between 18 and 25 years old. Be currently enrolled at an eligible partner university. Have an interest in local community impact. Have sufficient English-language skills to follow discussions and communicate with other participants. Be willing to collaborate across cultures, identities and perspectives. Commit approximately three to four hours per week. Participate actively in virtual and in-person activities. Complete required assignments and preparatory work. Preference is given to students who expect to remain at their university for at least two years after the program begins. This supports continued participation in campus teams and long-term local activities. Eligible Partner Universities Only students currently enrolled at the following institutions may apply: Ashesi University, Accra, Ghana B.M.S. Group of Institutions, Bangalore, India Universidad de La Frontera, Temuco, Chile Friedrich Schiller University, Jena, Germany Dillard University, New Orleans, United States Students at other universities are not eligible for this particular program, even if they meet the age requirement. They may instead consider the Global Solvers Accelerator if they are aged 20–35 and have an eligible community initiative. Global Citizens’ Connect Actively engaged participants may attend the Global Citizens’ Connect, a fully sponsored, week-long international gathering. The Foundation states that travel, accommodation and participation costs are covered for eligible, actively engaged participants. The gathering brings the cohort together for workshops, intercultural exchange, community engagement and collaborative work on global challenges. Participation is not intended as tourism or recreational travel. Fellows should expect intensive learning, unfamiliar environments, shared spaces, local food, collaborative responsibilities and structured activities. Cost and Financial Coverage The Global Citizenship Learning Program has no program fee. Virtual learning activities are free, and the costs associated with the Global Citizens’ Connect are covered for participants who remain actively engaged and are invited to attend. Applicants should nevertheless review final participation terms and travel instructions if selected, particularly regarding passports, visas, local transportation and any personal incidental expenses. Application Process Applicants must complete an online form containing questions about their experiences, perspectives, motivations, leadership potential and commitment to community impact. All answers must: Be written in English. Remain within the specified word limits. Be complete. Be submitted before the deadline. Reflect the applicant’s authentic experiences and voice. The Foundation permits applicants to use artificial-intelligence tools for limited language polishing, but warns against using them to generate the entire application. Applications that appear wholly AI-generated may be eliminated. Applicants can use the GCLP 2027 Application Guide to prepare their responses before entering them in the online form. GCLP Selection Process The selection process involves several stages: Submission of the online application. Initial screening by the relevant partner university. Local assessment or interview, primarily conducted in English. Nomination of leading candidates for a Global Virtual Assessment Centre. Assessment of teamwork, problem-solving, communication and understanding of global challenges. Final selection by an international selection team. Approximately 20 students are expected to join the cohort. Shortlisted applicants may be invited to a 120-minute virtual Assessment Centre in late January or early February 2027, with final results expected by the end of February 2027. Applicants should regularly check their email and spam folders and monitor notices from their university’s Melton Foundation campus team. GCLP Application Deadline Applications opened on 15 August 2026 and close on: 15 November 2026 at 11:59 p.m. US Eastern Standard Time Applicants should account for the time-zone difference and avoid waiting until the final day. Eligible students may submit the Global Citizenship Learning Program 2027 application here . Which Melton Foundation Program Should You Choose? Choose the Global Solvers Accelerator if you: Are between 20 and 35 years old. Can apply from any country. Already have a community or social-impact project. Want to strengthen that project through international peer learning. Can pay the program fee or obtain partial need-based support. Choose the Global Citizenship Learning Program if you: Are between 18 and 25 years old. Are enrolled at one of the five designated partner universities. Want to build global citizenship and leadership skills. Have strong motivation but may not yet have an established social-impact record. Want to participate in a completely free ten-month learning program. Application Tips for Both Programs Select the correct pathway Do not apply solely because both opportunities lead to the Melton Fellowship. Your age, university status and existing project determine which option is appropriate. Provide specific evidence Use concrete examples of community involvement, leadership, challenges, learning and impact. Avoid unsupported claims and generic statements. Explain your motivation clearly Show why global citizenship, sustainable development and intercultural collaboration matter to your work or future goals. Be honest about challenges The Foundation values reflection and learning potential. Explain what you still need to learn and how the program could help you address real limitations. Protect your authentic voice Prepare your responses personally. Any language support should preserve your ideas, experiences and natural writing style. Prepare early Application forms are detailed. Draft answers offline, respect the word limits and collect references or financial-support documents before the deadline. Confirm your availability Both programs require consistent participation. Consider your academic, employment and project responsibilities before committing. title: NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship 2027: $30,000 Funding for Doctoral Researchers in Education
summary: Applications are now open for the NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship 2027 , a highly competitive doctoral funding opportunity supporting emerging scholars whose dissertation research can contribute to the improvement and understanding of education. Administered by the National Academy of Education (NAEd) with support from the Spencer Foundation , the fellowship is designed for doctoral candidates at graduate schools in the United States who are entering the dissertation-writing stage of their degree. Each year, approximately 35 outstanding doctoral researchers are selected for the fellowship. Successful applicants receive $30,000 , normally supporting one academic year of dissertation writing, alongside professional development retreats and mentorship from an established scholar. The fellowship welcomes applicants from a remarkably broad range of academic disciplines. Candidates do not need to study in a school or department of education, provided their dissertation is centrally concerned with education and they can demonstrate how their research will contribute to the field. Applications opened on August 1, 2026 , and the application deadline is October 8, 2026 at 5:00 PM Eastern Time . The earliest fellowship start date is September 1, 2027 . About the NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship The NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship was created to encourage a new generation of scholars from different academic disciplines and professional backgrounds to undertake innovative research relevant to improving education. Rather than limiting support to conventional education departments, the fellowship recognizes that important educational research emerges from many fields. Eligible dissertations may bring new perspectives to the: History of education Theory of education Analysis of education Practice and application of education Formal educational systems Informal education Educational institutions Learning outside traditional school environments Educational policy Social, cultural, political, economic, or historical dimensions of education The programme is specifically looking for dissertations that provide innovative, insightful and rigorous approaches to educational questions . Fellowship Value Successful fellows receive: $30,000 for one academic year The award is distributed in two installments . The funding is primarily intended to give doctoral candidates the time and financial flexibility necessary to concentrate on writing their dissertations rather than relying heavily on outside employment. Importantly, this is not simply a cash award. The fellowship includes three major components: Financial support Professional development retreats Individual academic mentorship Approximately 35 Fellows Selected Each Year The NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship is highly competitive. Each year, the programme identifies approximately: 35 fellows from among doctoral candidates conducting dissertation research relevant to education. The selection process involves multiple rounds of review by scholars and a fellowship selection committee. Applicants should therefore approach the application as a serious academic research competition rather than as a general financial-aid programme. Three Major Components of the Fellowship 1. $30,000 Financial Award The $30,000 award helps fellows devote significant time to dissertation writing. The programme is specifically intended to reduce the need for extensive employment during the dissertation phase. Funding is paid in two installments over the fellowship period. 2. Professional Development Retreats Fellows participate in two professional development retreats facilitated by members of the National Academy of Education and other distinguished scholars. The retreats include both general and specialized discussions intended to strengthen: Research skills Scholarly development Academic writing Intellectual engagement Professional growth The retreats also provide selected fellows with an opportunity to engage with other researchers at similar stages of their academic careers. 3. Mentorship Each fellow selects an: NAEd member, or Another distinguished scholar to serve as a mentor during the fellowship year. This mentorship component provides ongoing academic guidance and professional support as fellows work toward completing their dissertations. Who Can Apply for the NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship? Applicants must satisfy several important requirements. To be eligible, candidates must: Be candidates for a doctoral degree at a graduate school within the United States. Complete all pre-dissertation requirements by June 1, 2027 . Provide a clear plan demonstrating that the dissertation can be completed within one or two years. Propose an education-related research project. Apply individually rather than as part of a group application. U.S. Citizenship Is Not Required One of the most important aspects of the fellowship is that applicants do not need to be U.S. citizens . International doctoral students can apply as long as they are candidates for a doctoral degree at an eligible graduate institution within the United States. The programme s FAQ further clarifies that non-U.S. citizens are eligible if they are doctoral candidates at a U.S. graduate school. However, international universities that merely have charters or other arrangements in the United States do not satisfy this eligibility requirement. What Counts as Education Research? The NAEd and Spencer Foundation use a broad understanding of education. Education can include: Formal education Non-formal education Early childhood education Primary education Secondary education Higher education Adult education Learning inside schools Learning outside schools U.S.-based education Education outside the United States This means applicants are not restricted to research taking place in American schools. A doctoral student enrolled at a U.S. graduate school may potentially conduct research concerning education in another country or region, provided the applicant clearly explains the educational significance of the research. You Do Not Need to Be in an Education Department Applicants from any academic discipline may apply. The fellowship has previously supported doctoral researchers from fields including: Anthropology Architecture Art history Communications Economics Education History Linguistics Literature Philosophy Political science Psychology Public health Religion Sociology This list is not exhaustive. Candidates from other disciplines are also encouraged to apply if they can demonstrate that their dissertation is fundamentally relevant to education. For example, a political science dissertation could be relevant if it examines education policy, educational inequality, school governance, or the political consequences of educational institutions. Similarly, research in anthropology might investigate educational practices within communities, while public-health research could explore school-based interventions or health education. The critical issue is not the applicant s department but the central relevance of the dissertation to education . Long-Term Interest in Education Research Applicants should also demonstrate that their engagement with education is not merely incidental. The fellowship expects candidates to show interest in continuing to conduct educational research after earning their doctorate. Selection committees consider whether applicants appear likely to remain active scholars whose future work will continue contributing to education research. Pre-Dissertation Requirements All pre-dissertation requirements must be completed by: June 1, 2027 These requirements include: Coursework Qualifying papers Comprehensive examinations Formal approval of the dissertation proposal Any other programme-specific candidacy requirements The fellowship is intended to finance the writing stage of the dissertation , not coursework or early doctoral preparation. Applicants who will still be completing substantial coursework or other candidacy requirements after June 1, 2027 would therefore not meet this requirement. Fellowship Duration Although the award is generally described as supporting one academic year, the allowable tenure can vary. The fellowship may last: Not less than nine months and not more than 24 months. Applicants submit a work plan explaining how they expect to complete their dissertation. The earliest possible fellowship start date is: September 1, 2027 Candidates must demonstrate that the dissertation can realistically be completed within the time proposed. Full-Time and Part-Time Fellowship Options The standard model supports approximately one year of full-time dissertation writing . However, applicants who cannot work full-time on their dissertations may propose a longer work plan of up to two years. This can accommodate: Part-time dissertation work Alternating periods of dissertation writing and income-producing employment Regardless of the structure chosen, candidates are expected to present clear milestones and demonstrate that their dissertation can be completed within the proposed timeframe. What the Fellowship Does Not Primarily Fund Applicants should understand that this fellowship is focused heavily on dissertation writing . It is not primarily intended to finance: Coursework Early-stage doctoral preparation Major new data-collection projects Candidates should generally have progressed far enough in their dissertation that the fellowship can support completion of analysis and writing. This timing requirement is central to the programme. What Can the $30,000 Be Used For? The fellowship gives recipients considerable discretion over how to use the funding. Funds may potentially support: Living expenses Medical insurance Dental insurance Research equipment Research expenses Books Workshops Conferences University tuition University fees The core purpose, however, remains to support the fellow while completing the dissertation. Can Fellows Work During the Fellowship? Some employment is possible. The NAEd recognizes that fellows have different personal and financial circumstances. However, the fellowship recommends that fellows work: No more than approximately 10 hours per week during the award period. Applicants who intend to work should seek approval from NAEd staff. The purpose of the fellowship is to reduce the need for substantial employment so that candidates can focus on completing the dissertation. Can Fellows Hold Other Funding? Applicants are allowed to apply for other funding opportunities. Applying for additional scholarships or fellowships does not automatically affect eligibility. However, rules apply if a candidate receives another award. In general: External fellowships normally cannot be held concurrently with the NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship. Certain internal university or departmental fellowships may potentially be held simultaneously. Candidates must notify NAEd staff and obtain approval. Examples of external awards mentioned in the programme guidance include the Ford Foundation Predoctoral Fellowship and AERA Minority Dissertation Fellowship. Selection Priorities The dissertation must focus primarily on education. However, the fellowship does not privilege a single methodology, discipline, geographical region, or educational setting. Applicants should instead demonstrate that their project: Addresses a meaningful educational question Is grounded in relevant scholarship and theory Uses an appropriate research methodology Can generate new knowledge Has a feasible completion plan Shows evidence of the applicant s potential as an education researcher Core Evaluation Criteria The selection committee identifies three fundamental criteria. 1. Importance of the Research Question The proposed research question should address an issue that matters to education. Applicants should explain: Why the problem deserves study What is currently unknown Why the question matters How answering it may improve understanding of education 2. Quality and Feasibility of the Research Approach Candidates need more than an interesting topic. They must demonstrate that the research design and work plan are appropriate and realistic. The committee examines issues including: Research design Sources of evidence Measurement Classification Data analysis Interpretation Methodological appropriateness 3. Future Research Potential The committee also considers the applicant s future potential as a researcher. Applicants should demonstrate a credible commitment to continuing scholarly work related to education after the doctorate. What Reviewers Look for in the Dissertation Proposal Reviewers consider whether applicants demonstrate strong knowledge of relevant research and theory. They assess: Whether the proposal is grounded in appropriate scholarship Whether the educational relevance is convincing Whether the research can generate new knowledge Whether the methodology is clearly explained Whether methods fit the research question Whether preliminary findings support the project s feasibility, where available Whether the dissertation is likely to contribute meaningfully to education research Whether the proposal is clearly organized and well written Whether the candidate can finish within the fellowship period Whether the candidate appears likely to continue conducting education research Clear academic writing is therefore itself part of the assessment. Application Review Process Applications go through a multi-stage evaluation process. Stage 1: Administrative Screening Staff first review applications for: Completeness Eligibility Fit with the fellowship s education-research focus Applications without a convincing educational focus may not progress. Stage 2: Disciplinary Review Two senior scholars from the applicant s discipline evaluate the application. The fellowship states that approximately half of applications do not progress beyond this stage. Stage 3: Selection Committee Review The remaining applications are reviewed by the selection committee. Each application is evaluated by two committee members. Approximately: 60 semifinalists are then selected. Semifinalists are asked to provide updated information regarding: Research progress Timeline Budget Other relevant developments Stage 4: Final Selection Remaining applications receive further review, with each application evaluated by five committee members. Approximately: 35 finalists/fellows are ultimately selected. Application Components The NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship requires a substantial application. Applicants should prepare well before the October deadline. 1. Background Information The online application asks candidates to provide information including: Demographic information Education history Employment history Scholarships received Fellowships received Assistantships received Other funding applications Honors and awards Publications Presentations Pre-dissertation requirement status Language proficiency 2. Personal Statement Applicants must submit a personal statement discussing how their previous academic and educational experiences prepared them to conduct the proposed dissertation research. The statement should also explain: Intended career path Professional and academic goals Whether the applicant expects to remain engaged in education research How the dissertation fits into longer-term scholarly development 3. Dissertation Work Plan Applicants must provide a detailed work plan. The fellowship expects candidates to explain: Proposed fellowship start date Proposed fellowship end date Data-analysis milestones Chapter-completion dates Expected date for submitting the dissertation to the committee Other relevant dissertation milestones Applicants may also include important activities that will occur before the fellowship begins. A realistic work plan is extremely important because the committee must believe the dissertation can be completed within the proposed fellowship period. 4. Dissertation Abstract Applicants must prepare a concise, single-spaced abstract. The abstract should summarize: Substantive focus Research design Purpose Methods Scope Contribution to education 5. Narrative Discussion The dissertation narrative is one of the most important components of the application. Applicants may submit: Up to 10 double-spaced pages with: One-inch margins At least 11-point Times New Roman font Page numbers Applicant s full name Applicant s email address in a running header The narrative should clearly explain: Project goals Contribution to the field Significance of the research Relevance to education Theoretical framework Relevant literature Research questions Research design Data-collection methods Data-analysis methods Interpretation techniques Where preliminary results or pilot findings are available, applicants may briefly discuss them. The programme specifically warns that insufficient clarity about how data will be treated in relation to the research questions can weaken an application. 6. Bibliography Applicants should append a: Maximum two-page, single-spaced bibliography containing the most important sources related to the dissertation. The narrative and bibliography should be uploaded together as one document. The combined maximum is: 12 pages Technical or supplemental appendices may be included without counting against the page limit, but applicants are advised to use them carefully because reviewers are not required to examine supplemental materials. 7. Graduate Transcript Applicants must upload a graduate transcript. An: Unofficial transcript is acceptable. 8. Two Letters of Recommendation Exactly two recommendation letters are required. They must include: One letter from the applicant s dissertation director or chair One letter from another faculty member Recommenders must submit their letters online. The fellowship will accept only two letters per applicant, and recommendation letters have the same deadline as the main application . Extensions are not provided. Applicants should therefore contact their referees well before October 8. What Recommenders Are Asked to Discuss Recommendation letters should address: The recommender s relationship with the applicant How the candidate compares with other students Strength of the proposed dissertation Educational relevance of the project Relationship to existing research Potential contribution to the literature Candidate s potential as a scholar Likelihood of continuing education research Potential long-term contribution to educational scholarship Writing for Both Specialists and Generalists An important application-writing consideration is that proposals are reviewed by both scholars who know the applicant s discipline well and reviewers who may be less familiar with its terminology. Applicants should therefore avoid unnecessarily specialized language. Discipline-specific concepts should be clearly situated within an argument that a broader academic audience can understand. A competitive proposal should be sophisticated enough for a specialist but accessible enough for an interdisciplinary committee. Can Three-Article Dissertations Apply? Yes. The fellowship accepts applications for dissertations using a three-article format . However, the NAEd does not provide a separate template specifically for article-based dissertations. Applicants should focus on making the proposal a cohesive document that clearly communicates the central idea and overarching contribution of the dissertation. Can Previous Applicants Reapply? Yes. Candidates who previously applied unsuccessfully may reapply as long as they continue to meet the eligibility criteria. A reapplicant must submit a new application . Application Deadline The deadline for the NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship 2027 is: October 8, 2026 at 5:00 PM Eastern Time Applications opened on: August 1, 2026 The earliest fellowship start date is: September 1, 2027 Applicants should also remember that recommendation letters must be submitted by the same deadline. Because the application requires a substantial dissertation narrative, personal statement, work plan, transcript, bibliography and two recommendations, candidates should begin preparing well in advance. How to Apply Applications must be submitted through the official online portal. Official application portal: https://naedfellowships.secure-platform.com/a/page/dissertationfellowship Applicants should ensure that every required component is complete before submitting. Questions about the programme can be directed to: info@naeducation.org Helpful Proposal-Writing Resources The Spencer Foundation provides several resources that applicants may find useful when developing their proposals. These include guides on: Writing successful research grant proposals Communicating qualitative research design Preparing quantitative proposals The programme emphasizes that a strong application should present a well-grounded and convincing argument built around an innovative and important research idea, accompanied by methods that effectively address the proposed questions. Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application 1. Make Education Central Do not simply mention education briefly because the fellowship requires it. Reviewers must be convinced that the dissertation genuinely advances understanding of education. Clearly explain: What educational issue you study Why it matters What existing literature does not adequately explain What new contribution your research makes 2. Show a Clear Research Gap A strong proposal should identify the unresolved question or intellectual problem motivating the dissertation. Avoid describing only the topic. Instead, demonstrate why additional research is needed. 3. Explain Your Methods Carefully Do not assume reviewers will infer how the research works. Clearly describe: Evidence Data Sampling Sources Coding Analysis Interpretation where relevant. 4. Write for an Interdisciplinary Audience Your proposal may be evaluated by scholars outside your narrow specialization. Explain important terminology and theoretical concepts without oversimplifying the intellectual argument. 5. Present a Realistic Completion Plan This is a dissertation-completion fellowship. The committee needs to believe that you are sufficiently advanced to finish the dissertation during or shortly after the fellowship. Build a credible month-by-month or stage-by-stage timeline. 6. Demonstrate Future Research Potential Explain how the dissertation connects to your long-term scholarly trajectory. The fellowship is specifically designed to cultivate a new generation of education researchers. 7. Request Recommendation Letters Early Your referees face the same October 8 deadline. Do not wait until the final week. Give recommenders: Your dissertation summary Research proposal CV Draft personal statement Deadline information Clear submission instructions well in advance. Why the NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship Matters The fellowship combines financial support with professional development and scholarly mentorship at an important stage of a doctoral researcher s career. Many doctoral candidates face significant pressure during the dissertation-writing period as they balance research with teaching, employment, caregiving or other responsibilities. The $30,000 award is designed to reduce some of that pressure and create greater space for sustained dissertation work. At the same time, the programme connects fellows with accomplished scholars and peers from different disciplines, allowing them to develop intellectual and professional relationships that may continue beyond the fellowship year. The broad disciplinary eligibility also makes the programme particularly valuable for researchers studying education from unconventional or interdisciplinary perspectives. Important Facts at a Glance Programme: NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship Application status: Accepting applications Career stage: Doctoral Number selected: Approximately 35 fellows annually Funding: $30,000 Payment: Two installments Duration: Generally one academic year; permitted tenure ranges from nine to 24 months Earliest start: September 1, 2027 Application opened: August 1, 2026 Deadline: October 8, 2026 at 5:00 PM ET Citizenship requirement: U.S. citizenship not required Institutional requirement: Applicant must be a doctoral candidate at a graduate school within the United States Research requirement: Dissertation must focus primarily on education Pre-dissertation requirements: Must be completed by June 1, 2027 Recommendations: Two letters required Contact: info@naeducation.org Conclusion The NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship 2027 is an exceptional opportunity for advanced doctoral candidates whose research can contribute meaningfully to the understanding or improvement of education. Approximately 35 fellows are selected annually, with each recipient receiving $30,000 , participation in two professional-development retreats and access to scholarly mentorship. The fellowship is especially notable for its interdisciplinary approach. Applicants may come from anthropology, history, political science, economics, sociology, psychology, public health, literature, linguistics, architecture, communications, education or virtually any other discipline, as long as education remains central to the dissertation. International students are also eligible. U.S. citizenship is not required , although applicants must be doctoral candidates at graduate schools located within the United States. Successful applicants need more than an interesting research topic. They must demonstrate an important educational research question, rigorous and appropriate methodology, a convincing contribution to the field, a realistic dissertation-completion plan and strong potential for a future research career. Candidates must complete all pre-dissertation requirements by June 1, 2027 , and the fellowship is intended primarily to support dissertation writing rather than coursework or major new data collection. Applications close on October 8, 2026 at 5:00 PM Eastern Time . Given the competitiveness of the programme and the substantial application requirements, prospective candidates should begin preparing their dissertation narrative, personal statement, work plan and recommendation requests well before the deadline.
