title: Globe and Mail Foundation Scholarship for Syrian Media Professionals: Online Journalism Fellowship at the University of Toronto
summary: The Globe and Mail Foundation Scholarship for a Syrian Media Professional offers a unique opportunity for a Syrian media worker to receive advanced journalism training, professional mentorship and international reporting experience through the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana Fellowship in Journalism and Health Impact . The part-time fellowship is designed to help a Syrian media professional strengthen their journalism skills, develop stories for international audiences and build connections with global newsroom editors. The programme will run from September 8, 2026, to March 16, 2027 , and participants can complete the programme entirely online from anywhere in the world. About the Fellowship The Globe and Mail Foundation is partnering with the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana Fellowship in Journalism and Health Impact to support and train a Syrian media professional who wants to develop their career as a journalist working with Canadian and international media. The fellowship focuses on helping subject-matter specialists and media professionals learn how to turn their areas of expertise into effective reporting beats. Although the programme includes a strong health and journalism component, applicants are not limited to health-related specialties . The selected Fellow will have the opportunity to identify a reporting area that they want to develop and produce stories aimed at an international audience. The programme is particularly intended to provide professional support to a Syrian media professional during Syria’s transition and help them build the skills and experience needed to engage with global journalism platforms. What the Fellowship Provides The selected Fellow will receive training, mentorship and practical experience in several areas of journalism. Key areas include: Journalism training for international reporting Direct mentorship from programme faculty Guidance in finding and developing story ideas Support with pitching stories to editors Training in investigative journalism Training in AI for reporting Guidance on developing and maintaining a freelance journalism practice Career planning and professional development Opportunities to engage with an international journalism audience Additional support and mentorship from The Globe and Mail Foundation based on the Fellow’s needs A major component of the programme is the opportunity for the Fellow to find, pitch and report their own stories . This allows participants to move beyond classroom learning and develop practical experience in producing journalism for a broader international audience. Programme Format and Dates The fellowship is a part-time programme running from: September 8, 2026 – March 16, 2027 Participants do not have to relocate to Canada because the entire programme can be completed online. In-person attendance is not required , making the opportunity accessible to the selected Fellow regardless of their location. The programme consists of three main components: 1. Two-Week Journalism Bootcamp The programme begins with an intensive two-week bootcamp running from: September 8–18, 2026 The bootcamp provides the foundation for the fellowship and prepares participants for the subsequent training, reporting and mentorship activities. 2. Weekly Cohort Sessions From September 22, 2026, to March 16, 2027 , Fellows will participate in weekly full-cohort teaching and story meetings. These sessions provide opportunities to learn alongside other participants, discuss story ideas and receive guidance on journalism projects. 3. Monthly Skills Classes From October 2026 through March 2027 , Fellows will participate in skills classes held on one Friday/Saturday pair each month. These sessions will focus on practical journalism skills that participants can apply to their reporting and professional careers. A Focus on International Journalism One of the central objectives of the fellowship is to help the selected Syrian media professional develop the ability to work with global newsroom editors and international audiences . The programme provides training in how to: Identify strong international story ideas Develop reporting beats Research and investigate stories Pitch stories effectively Produce journalism for international media Work with editors Build a professional journalism portfolio Develop a sustainable freelance practice This makes the fellowship particularly valuable for a media professional who wants to expand beyond local or regional reporting and begin contributing to international media. Who Can Apply? The opportunity is specifically designed for a Syrian media professional . Applicants should: Be a media professional from Syria Have a good working knowledge of English Have an interest in international journalism and reporting Be able to participate in the part-time programme from September 2026 to March 2027 Be prepared to develop and pitch their own story ideas Have an interest in developing a reporting beat for Canadian or international media The source information does not specify a minimum academic qualification, age requirement or particular university degree. Applicants who have previous reporting experience may submit up to three reporting clips , although this is optional. The clips may be submitted in Arabic . APPLY HERE Application Requirements Applicants must submit their application by email and provide the required materials in English. The application should include: 1. CV Applicants must submit an English-language CV highlighting their professional and media experience. 2. Letter of Intent Applicants must provide a 500-word Letter of Intent in English . The letter should describe the reporting beat they wish to cover . Applicants should therefore clearly explain the area they want to specialise in and why it is relevant to their journalism career. 3. Two Story Pitches Applicants must submit two story pitches in English . These pitches should demonstrate the applicant s ability to identify compelling stories and explain how they could be developed for an international audience. 4. Reporting Clips Applicants may submit up to three clips of their reporting . This component is optional , and the clips can be in Arabic . Application Deadline The deadline to apply is: Monday, August 24, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time (Toronto). Applicants should ensure that their complete application reaches the programme before the stated deadline. How to Apply Applications should be submitted by email to: Rob Steiner, Fellowship Director University of Toronto Email: robert.steiner@utoronto.ca Applicants should also copy: The Globe and Mail Foundation Email: education@globeandmailfoundation.com The application should contain the CV, Letter of Intent, two story pitches and, if available, up to three reporting clips. Visit HERE to learn more about the Globe and Mail Foundation Scholarship for Syrian Media Professionals Selection Process Applications will be assessed by a volunteer jury . Applicants should therefore ensure that their submissions clearly communicate their journalism experience, proposed reporting interests and ability to contribute to international media. Particular attention should be given to the quality of the proposed reporting beat and story pitches, as these materials demonstrate the applicant s ability to identify and develop stories. Why This Fellowship Matters The fellowship provides more than journalism training. It is designed to help a Syrian media professional develop the skills, professional relationships and confidence needed to work with international media. Through mentorship and practical reporting, the selected Fellow can develop experience in: International journalism Investigative reporting Story development Story pitching AI-assisted reporting Freelance journalism Professional newsroom engagement Career development The online format also means the selected Fellow can participate without being required to relocate to Canada. Conclusion The Globe and Mail Foundation Scholarship for a Syrian Media Professional is an opportunity for a Syrian media worker to strengthen their journalism career through the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana Fellowship in Journalism and Health Impact. Running from September 8, 2026, to March 16, 2027 , the part-time programme combines journalism training, direct mentorship, story development, international reporting and professional career guidance. Participants can complete the fellowship entirely online, making physical relocation unnecessary. Eligible Syrian media professionals with a strong working knowledge of English are encouraged to prepare their CV, 500-word Letter of Intent and two English-language story pitches before submitting their application. title: Emory University Climate Solutions Fellow 2026: One-Year Sustainability Fellowship in Atlanta
summary: Emory University is inviting qualified candidates to apply for the Fellow Climate Solutions – Campus Services position within its Office of Sustainability Initiatives (OSI) . The role offers an opportunity to contribute to university-wide climate and sustainability programmes, with a strong focus on student engagement, communications, events and sustainability initiatives. About the Climate Solutions Fellow Position The Climate Solutions Fellow will serve for an initial one-year term , with the possibility of renewal for up to three years. Student Engagement A major part of the position involves finding creative ways to engage Emory students in sustainability. Relationship and Network Development The Fellow will establish and maintain relationships with different groups both within and outside the university. Some climate- or sustainability-related extracurricular, training, educational or internship experience. Proficiency with Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint . Experience with climate action initiatives. Demonstrated social media proficiency. Graphic design experience. Interest in learning additional software. Experience working with students or student organizations. Strong programme coordination skills. Candidates who can combine sustainability knowledge with communication, digital media and student engagement skills may find the role particularly relevant. Location and Work Arrangement The position is based at: Emory University – Clifton Corridor Atlanta, Georgia, USA The role is classified as Hybrid Remote . The Fellow may work from home regularly but must be able to commute to Emory University on a flexible weekly schedule according to departmental needs . Qualified applicants receive consideration for employment without discrimination based on characteristics protected under applicable state or federal law, including race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability and protected veteran status. The university also states its commitment to providing reasonable accommodations and ensuring equal access for qualified individuals with disabilities. title: AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship 2026–2027: $5,000 Stipend, Policy Training and Frontier AI Governance Experience
summary: The AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship (PEF) 2026–2027 offers an opportunity for early- to mid-career professionals who want to turn ideas about frontier artificial intelligence safety, security and governance into practical policy solutions. Running from September 30, 2026, through February 28, 2027 , the fellowship is designed around policy entrepreneurship rather than academic research alone. Fellows will work part-time as affiliates of the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) , developing a concrete policy idea, engaging decision-makers, building coalitions and identifying realistic pathways for their proposal to influence policy. The fellowship provides a $5,000 stipend , with an opportunity for an additional $1,000 merit award for the Fellow who develops the most specific and actionable policy memo and advocacy plan. Selected travel expenses for required in-person events are also supported through an additional travel stipend. Applications must be submitted by 11:59 PM ET on September 7, 2026 . What Is the AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship? The Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship is an initiative designed to help participants move promising policy ideas beyond the conceptual stage and toward real-world implementation. Rather than concentrating exclusively on producing research papers, the fellowship emphasizes the practical process of making policy happen. Participants will be encouraged to: Identify an important policy problem. Develop a practical and implementable solution. Identify institutions capable of implementing the solution. Understand relevant decision-makers. Engage policymakers and other stakeholders. Build coalitions around their proposal. Identify opportunities or policy windows for action. Develop an advocacy strategy. Produce a policy memo. Move their idea toward practical policy adoption. For the 2026–2027 cohort, the fellowship will specifically focus on frontier AI safety issues . This makes the program particularly relevant to professionals interested in the intersection of artificial intelligence, public policy, national security, cybersecurity, governance, technology regulation and catastrophic risk management . Fellowship Focus: Frontier AI Safety The fellowship will explore policy challenges arising from increasingly capable and advanced AI systems. Fellows are encouraged to examine different dimensions of frontier AI safety, including technical, regulatory, institutional and governance challenges. Technical AI Safety One area of focus is ensuring that frontier AI systems are: Reliable. Predictable. Secure. Aligned with human values. Designed and deployed in ways that reduce serious risks. Applicants with technical AI expertise may therefore be able to translate their technical knowledge into policy proposals addressing the governance of advanced AI systems. AI Governance and Policy Another major area involves developing frameworks for governing the development and use of frontier AI. Potential questions may include: What policies should govern advanced AI development? Which institutions should oversee high-risk AI systems? How should governments establish appropriate safeguards? What regulatory mechanisms could reduce catastrophic AI risks? How can governments build the capacity required to govern rapidly developing technologies? Risk Assessment and Mitigation Fellows may also explore ways to identify, evaluate and reduce risks associated with increasingly capable AI systems. Potential policy approaches could involve: Risk assessment frameworks. Safety requirements. Risk classification systems. Governance mechanisms. Monitoring and oversight. Mitigation standards. Institutional preparedness. Transparency and Accountability The fellowship also welcomes ideas addressing transparency and accountability in AI development and deployment. This could include examining how governments, companies and other institutions can improve understanding of: How advanced AI systems are developed. What capabilities they possess. What risks they create. How they are deployed. Who is responsible for managing those risks. How oversight can be strengthened. Priority Policy Themes The fellowship is particularly interested in policy proposals addressing several emerging frontier AI safety and governance issues. These include: Cybersecurity Applicants could examine cybersecurity risks associated with advanced AI systems and develop policy mechanisms designed to strengthen security. Capability Thresholds Another potential area is determining whether specific AI capabilities should trigger additional regulatory, safety or oversight requirements. Risk Taxonomies Fellows may explore systems for categorizing different types and levels of AI risk so that policymakers can develop proportionate responses. Critical Infrastructure Advanced AI could have implications for critical infrastructure and essential systems. Policy proposals could examine how these risks should be assessed and mitigated. Compute Governance Computational resources play an important role in the development of frontier AI. Fellows may explore governance mechanisms relating to access to, monitoring of or oversight of advanced computing resources. Model Proliferation The fellowship is interested in questions surrounding the proliferation of AI models, including the policy implications of open versus closed systems . Policy Design and Government Capacity Applicants may also propose broader approaches to policy design, institutional arrangements and government capacity for managing catastrophic risks associated with advanced AI. What Is Expected From Fellows? The fellowship is designed to give participants flexibility to pursue a policy project that they believe can create meaningful impact. However, Fellows are expected to develop a concrete policy proposal rather than simply explore a broad research topic. The central objective is to identify a specific frontier AI safety problem and develop a feasible pathway toward policy adoption . Possible mechanisms for implementation could include: Legislation. Regulation. Government standards. Procurement requirements. Institutional design. Government policies. Governance frameworks. Other practical policy mechanisms. Key Fellowship Deliverable: Policy Memo One of the central responsibilities will be to develop and publish a policy memo addressing a specific frontier AI safety challenge. The memo should go beyond describing the problem. It should include: A clearly defined policy challenge. Evidence and analysis demonstrating why the issue matters. A practical policy solution. The institutions and decision-makers relevant to implementation. Key stakeholders who need to be engaged. A strategy for moving the proposal toward adoption. Consideration of practical barriers to implementation. The goal is to produce a policy document that can contribute to an actual policy conversation. Policy Entrepreneurship Training Fellows will participate in training sessions designed to strengthen their ability to turn ideas into policy impact. Training will address areas such as: Frontier AI safety. Policymaking processes. Policy entrepreneurship. Stakeholder engagement. Translating technical expertise into policy. Identifying policy opportunities. Building coalitions. Engaging decision-makers. Moving policy proposals toward implementation. Participants will also take part in reading groups intended to deepen their understanding of frontier AI safety and practical policymaking. In-Person California Retreat The fellowship includes an in-person California retreat tentatively scheduled for: November 4–7, 2026 The retreat will focus on: Mentorship. Community building. Developing fellowship projects. Advancing policy proposals. Connecting Fellows with relevant expertise and perspectives. An additional travel stipend will be available to cover selected expenses associated with the California retreat. Washington, DC Capstone Event Fellows are also expected to participate in an in-person capstone event in Washington, DC , tentatively scheduled for the week of: February 22, 2027 The capstone event is intended to provide an opportunity for Fellows to: Launch their policy memos. Disseminate their policy recommendations. Engage policymakers. Connect with experts. Engage relevant stakeholders. Present the outcomes of their fellowship projects. This component gives Fellows an opportunity to move their work beyond the fellowship itself and into conversations with people involved in policymaking and governance. Time Commitment The fellowship is structured as a part-time opportunity. Fellows are expected to dedicate an average of: 5 hours per week, or approximately 20 hours per month to the fellowship during the period from September 30, 2026, through February 28, 2027 . This time commitment includes mandatory fellowship programming. Participants will also take part in twice-monthly group check-ins . FAS will make reasonable efforts to schedule these sessions at times that accommodate participants. Select absences may be accommodated when participants provide appropriate notice, including absences related to: Illness. Work conflicts. Vacation. Exceptional circumstances may also be considered when determining whether a participant can be exempted from certain mandatory sessions. Individual Mentorship Each Fellow will receive individual support from FAS. The fellowship includes: Monthly individual check-ins with a dedicated FAS staff mentor. Additional meetings when needed. Additional communication and support as projects develop. Assistance connecting Fellows with relevant experts and policy actors. This mentorship component is particularly valuable for applicants who have strong technical or subject-matter expertise but limited experience navigating policy processes. Fellowship Benefits The AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship provides several professional and financial benefits. $5,000 Fellowship Stipend Each Fellow will receive a: $5,000 stipend This provides financial support for participants during the fellowship period. Additional $1,000 Merit Award An additional: $1,000 merit award may be provided to the Fellow whose policy memo and advocacy plan are judged to be the most specific and actionable. This means that participants have an opportunity to receive up to $6,000 in total financial awards , excluding eligible travel support. Travel Support An additional travel stipend will help cover selected expenses associated with: The California retreat. The Washington, DC capstone event. Professional Editing Fellows will receive professional editing support for written products developed during the fellowship. This can help improve the clarity, structure and professional quality of policy-related writing. Policy Engagement Training Participants will receive training from FAS staff focused on practical policy entrepreneurship. This can help Fellows understand how to move from research and ideas toward policy influence. Access to FAS Programming Fellows will receive invitations to relevant FAS programming. They will also have access to curated updates concerning the rapidly evolving federal science and technology policy landscape. Deep-Dive Sessions Participants will take part in interactive sessions examining practical aspects of policy entrepreneurship. These sessions can help Fellows better understand how policy processes work in practice. Expert Connections FAS will support Fellows in connecting with relevant experts and policy actors. This can help participants expand their professional networks and identify individuals and institutions that could contribute to their policy projects. Who Is the Fellowship Designed For? The fellowship is particularly well suited to early- to mid-career professionals who have strong subject-matter expertise but limited direct experience working in public policy. The program is intended for people who want to learn how to translate their knowledge into practical policy impact. Potential applicant backgrounds include: Technical AI research. Artificial intelligence. Academia. Think tanks. Civil society. Technology industry. Law. Cybersecurity. National security. Public policy. Science and technology policy. Related technical or policy disciplines. The fellowship is not limited to people who have previously worked as professional policymakers. In fact, candidates with substantial expertise in another field who want to learn how to translate that expertise into policy action may be particularly well suited to the program. Selection Criteria Applications will be assessed holistically. The selection process will consider the overall strength of the applicant and their proposed policy project rather than relying on a single qualification. 1. Understanding of a Significant AI Safety Challenge Applicants should demonstrate a clear understanding of an important frontier AI safety, security or governance problem. The problem should be meaningful and sufficiently specific to support a practical policy intervention. 2. Concrete Policy Idea Applicants should propose a concrete policy idea rather than simply identifying a broad concern about AI. The proposal should be: Specific. Practical. Implementation-oriented. Connected to a real policy challenge. Supported by a credible pathway toward adoption. 3. Understanding of Key Stakeholders Applicants should consider which institutions, decision-makers and stakeholders would be necessary to implement their proposal. This demonstrates that the applicant understands policy as a process involving multiple actors rather than simply producing a recommendation. 4. Understanding of Practical Policy Challenges Strong candidates should recognize that good policy ideas can face significant implementation barriers. Applicants should demonstrate willingness to think constructively about: Political constraints. Institutional limitations. Stakeholder interests. Implementation challenges. Government capacity. Competing priorities. Practical pathways toward adoption. 5. Curiosity and Initiative The fellowship seeks people who demonstrate curiosity, initiative and genuine interest in translating ideas into practical impact. Applicants should demonstrate that they are prepared to take initiative rather than simply conduct research. What Makes a Strong Application? A competitive application should clearly connect problem, solution and implementation . A strong proposal should answer questions such as: What specific frontier AI safety problem are you addressing? Why is this problem important? Who is affected by the problem? What policy intervention are you proposing? Which institution could implement it? Who are the relevant decision-makers? Which stakeholders would support or oppose it? What barriers could prevent implementation? How could those barriers be addressed? What practical opportunity exists for advancing the proposal? The strongest applications are therefore likely to demonstrate not only knowledge of AI safety but also an understanding of how policy change actually occurs. Why the Fellowship Is Valuable for AI Policy Careers The rapid development of frontier AI is creating increasing demand for professionals who understand both technology and public policy. However, technical expertise alone does not necessarily translate into policy influence. This fellowship addresses that gap by helping participants develop the skills required to move from: Technical or subject-matter expertise → Policy idea → Stakeholder engagement → Advocacy → Policy adoption Participants can therefore develop capabilities in: Policy analysis. Policy writing. Stakeholder mapping. Coalition building. Decision-maker engagement. Advocacy strategy. Policy communication. Governance. AI safety. Science and technology policy. For professionals considering long-term careers in AI governance, technology policy, national security, cybersecurity or public-interest technology, these capabilities can be particularly valuable. Click HERE to read more. Fellowship Timeline The fellowship runs for approximately five months. Fellowship begins: September 30, 2026 California retreat: November 4–7, 2026, tentatively Washington, DC capstone: Week of February 22, 2027, tentatively Fellowship concludes: February 28, 2027 Application deadline: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET Application Deadline and Submission Requirements Applications must be submitted by: 11:59 PM ET on September 7, 2026 Applicants should be aware that applications are accepted only through the designated application platform . When applicants select the application link, they will be redirected to the relevant platform and will need to create an account in order to submit their application. Candidates should therefore avoid waiting until the final hours to begin the application process. APPLY NOW! Important Application Considerations Before applying, candidates should make sure their proposed project is sufficiently focused. A broad proposal such as AI safety should be improved is unlikely to demonstrate the level of specificity expected from a policy entrepreneurship fellowship. Instead, applicants should identify a concrete problem and explain how a particular policy mechanism could address it. For example, a proposal might focus on: A specific cybersecurity risk associated with frontier AI. A governance mechanism for AI capability thresholds. A framework for categorizing advanced AI risks. AI risks to critical infrastructure. Governance of computing resources. Oversight of AI model proliferation. Standards for high-risk AI systems. Institutional capacity for managing catastrophic AI risks. The proposal should then connect the problem to a realistic implementation pathway. Conclusion The AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship 2026–2027 offers an opportunity for professionals to develop practical solutions to some of the emerging governance challenges associated with frontier artificial intelligence. The fellowship is particularly distinctive because it goes beyond traditional research. Participants are expected to identify a concrete policy problem, develop an actionable solution, understand the institutions and stakeholders involved, build relationships with decision-makers and pursue a realistic pathway toward implementation. With a $5,000 stipend, potential $1,000 merit award, travel support, professional editing, policy training, mentorship and access to experts , the program provides both financial and professional support for participants seeking to develop careers at the intersection of AI safety and public policy. Professionals from technical AI research, academia, cybersecurity, law, national security, civil society, industry, think tanks and related fields are encouraged to consider applying, particularly if they have a strong policy idea but limited direct experience navigating policymaking. title: Council of Europe Citizens’ Assemblies Workshop 2026 in Budapest: Apply for the Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies Training
summary: The Council of Europe Youth Department , together with the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe and in partnership with DemNet Foundation , has opened applications for an international capacity-building workshop on Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies . Titled “Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies: How to Start?” , the workshop will take place from 19 to 21 October 2026 at the European Youth Centre Budapest, Hungary . This opportunity is designed for young activists, civil society representatives, local and regional government representatives, youth-centre staff, political education practitioners and other people who are interested in democratic participation and have a concrete interest in establishing citizens’ assemblies or other deliberative processes. The workshop will provide practical training on how citizens’ assemblies work, how they can be planned and implemented, and how organisations and local or regional authorities can develop the institutional and political support needed to make such processes successful. Selected participants will have their travel, accommodation and meals covered for the duration of the workshop, in accordance with Council of Europe rules. The application deadline is 7 September 2026 . Opportunity Overview Opportunity: Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies: How to Start? Organisers: Council of Europe Youth Department and Congress of Local and Regional Authorities Partner: DemNet Foundation Opportunity type: International capacity-building workshop Location: European Youth Centre Budapest, Hungary Workshop dates: 19–21 October 2026 Expected arrival: 18 October 2026 Departure: 21 October 2026 Application deadline: 7 September 2026 Participants: Approximately 30 Minimum age: 18 Nationality requirement: Citizen of a Council of Europe member state Working language: English English requirement: Working-level English Travel: Covered for selected participants Accommodation: Covered for selected participants Meals: Covered for selected participants Application: Online application form The official call confirms that applications submitted after 7 September 2026 cannot be considered. What Is the Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies Workshop? Citizens’ assemblies are a form of deliberative democracy in which ordinary citizens are brought together to learn about an issue, consider different perspectives, deliberate collectively and develop recommendations. They can provide communities with structured ways of involving citizens in important public decisions. The Council of Europe workshop is designed to move beyond simply explaining the concept of citizens’ assemblies. It is a hands-on capacity-building experience intended to help participants understand what is required to actually design and implement one. According to the official call, participants should leave the workshop with a strong understanding of: How citizens’ assemblies work How to plan and organise an assembly How to develop an appropriate question or topic How to establish effective governance arrangements How to recruit participants How to facilitate the deliberative process How information and recommendations are handled How to connect the process with public administration How to build political and institutional support How citizens’ assemblies can operate at local and regional levels The workshop will particularly focus on helping participants take these ideas back to their own organisations, municipalities, regions or communities. Why Is This Workshop Being Organised? The workshop forms part of the Council of Europe programme “Strengthening Democratic Resilience through Youth Engagement and Deliberative Democracy.” The programme was launched in September 2025 and is scheduled to continue through May 2027. Its broader objective is to strengthen awareness and practical capacity for deliberative democracy, with a particular emphasis on youth citizens’ assemblies , across Council of Europe member states. The initiative builds on several important European democratic participation frameworks, including the Committee of Ministers recommendation on deliberative democracy, the Congress s recommendations concerning deliberative methods in European municipalities and regions, and the European Charter on the Participation of Young People in Local and Regional Life . The workshop therefore sits within a wider effort to strengthen democratic participation and create more meaningful opportunities for young people and citizens to contribute to public decision-making. What Will Participants Learn? The workshop is structured around practical learning rather than theoretical discussion alone. Participants will explore the complete process of developing a citizens’ assembly, from the initial concept through to implementation and follow-up. 1. Understanding Citizens’ Assemblies The first stage will introduce participants to the concept of citizens’ assemblies and the principles that make them effective. Participants will examine: What citizens’ assemblies are How they function Their key democratic principles Why deliberative approaches can complement traditional democratic processes Examples of citizens’ assemblies in different European countries Case studies from Ireland, France, Germany and other European contexts will be used to illustrate how deliberative processes have been applied in practice. 2. Planning a Citizens’ Assembly Participants will learn about the important decisions that must be made before launching an assembly. This includes: Framing the question Defining the purpose of the assembly Establishing governance arrangements Developing a recruitment approach Considering the roles of different stakeholders Preparing an appropriate structure for deliberation Participants will also participate in group work where they begin drafting their own citizens’ assembly proposal . This makes the workshop particularly relevant to people who already have an idea for a deliberative process in their municipality, organisation, region or community. 3. Moving From Planning to Practice The second seminar day will focus on what happens after the initial planning stage. Participants will explore the “in-between” phase of a citizens’ assembly, including: Providing participants with information Supporting deliberation Facilitation Developing recommendations Following up on recommendations Connecting citizens’ assemblies with public administration Addressing local and regional considerations Participants will then work on finalising their proposed citizens’ assemblies and presenting them for feedback. 4. Local and Regional Democracy A major focus of the workshop is the application of deliberative democracy at the local and regional level . This is particularly relevant to: Municipal officials Local government representatives Regional authorities Youth-policy professionals Civil society organisations Community advocates The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities will contribute expertise on embedding deliberative processes within municipal and regional governance. This can help participants understand how citizens’ assemblies can move from an interesting democratic concept into a practical mechanism that can operate within existing institutions. Public Panel Discussion on Deliberative Democracy In addition to the two-day capacity-building workshop, participants will attend a high-level public panel discussion . The panel will bring together international and Hungarian experts and will be open to diplomatic, civil society, academic and municipal stakeholders. The discussion will address two broad areas: International evidence on citizens’ assemblies Citizens’ assemblies at the local level, including opportunities and how to get started For workshop participants, the panel will provide direct expert input that can inform the practical training sessions that follow. Who Can Apply? The official call identifies several categories of people who are particularly encouraged to apply. Young Activists and Civil Society Representatives Young people actively involved in: Democratic participation Youth organisations Civic advocacy Community engagement Democratic resilience Civil society initiatives may find the workshop particularly relevant. Local and Regional Government Representatives The programme also welcomes representatives of local and regional authorities who have responsibilities relating to: Citizen engagement Youth policy Democratic innovation Public participation Local governance These participants can potentially use the knowledge gained to introduce or strengthen participatory processes within their municipalities or regions. Youth Centre and Civil Society Organisation Staff Staff members working in youth centres and civil society organisations can also apply, particularly where their work involves democratic participation, civic education or participatory methodologies. Political Education Practitioners Staff of schools and organisations involved in political education who have an interest in participatory methods are also specifically included in the target group. People With an Existing Citizens’ Assembly Idea The opportunity is especially relevant to individuals who already have a concrete idea or project underway involving a citizens’ assembly or another deliberative process. The idea could relate to: A municipality A region A civil society organisation A youth organisation A community initiative Another relevant institution Having a concrete idea can help participants directly apply the workshop s practical learning to their own context. Eligibility Requirements The official call specifies several important eligibility conditions. Minimum Age Applicants must be at least 18 years old . Citizenship Applicants must be citizens of a Council of Europe member state . This is an important requirement. The opportunity is therefore not open globally to applicants from every country . English Language The workshop will be conducted in English , and participants are expected to have a working level of English . Applicants should therefore be comfortable participating in discussions, group work, presentations and other interactive activities in English. Interest and Motivation Applicants should be motivated to bring citizens’ assemblies or deliberative democracy processes into their own contexts. The programme is not simply looking for people who want to learn about democracy in general. It is specifically seeking people who can potentially use and apply the knowledge gained from the workshop. What Are the Benefits of Participating? The workshop provides several substantial benefits for selected participants. Practical Expert-Led Training Participants will receive two full days of practical, expert-led training focused on designing, planning and delivering citizens’ assemblies. Rather than only studying deliberative democracy conceptually, participants will work through practical steps that can be applied in their own communities and organisations. International Expert Exposure Participants will gain access to a high-level public panel featuring international and Hungarian experts working on deliberative democracy. This can provide insight into different approaches and experiences from across Europe. Local and Regional Governance Knowledge Participants will receive dedicated input from the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities on how deliberative processes can be integrated into municipal and regional governance. Development of a Practical Proposal A particularly valuable component is the structured group work. Participants will develop a citizens’ assembly proposal that is tailored to their own organisation or community and receive expert feedback on their work. This means participants can potentially leave Budapest with a much clearer roadmap for implementing a deliberative process. European Networking The programme will connect participants with a growing European network of people working on deliberative democracy. This can provide opportunities for: Knowledge exchange Professional networking Collaboration Sharing experiences Learning from other European contexts Future democratic participation initiatives Travel, Accommodation and Meals Covered One of the most significant benefits is that travel, accommodation and meals are fully covered for selected participants , in accordance with Council of Europe rules. Participants will be hosted at the European Youth Centre Budapest during the programme. This makes the opportunity particularly attractive to eligible applicants who may otherwise find international training in Europe financially difficult to attend. Programme Schedule The official programme includes arrival, two main training days, a public panel discussion and departure. Sunday, 18 October 2026 — Arrival Participants are expected to arrive in Budapest on the evening of Sunday, 18 October 2026 . Activities include: Registration Welcome dinner Participants will be hosted at the European Youth Centre Budapest. Monday, 19 October 2026 — Seminar Day 1 The first seminar day focuses on: What are citizens’ assemblies and how do you build one? Key activities include: Introduction to citizens’ assemblies Key principles Case studies from Ireland, France, Germany and other European contexts Question framing Governance Recruitment Group work Beginning to draft a citizens’ assembly proposal Tuesday, 20 October 2026 — Seminar Day 2 The second seminar focuses on: From planning to practice Participants will explore: Information Facilitation Recommendations Follow-up Connecting with administration Local and regional dimensions Finalising citizens’ assembly proposals Presenting proposals Next steps Tuesday, 20 October 2026 — Public Panel The same day will also feature the public panel discussion on deliberative democracy. The panel will examine international evidence and the practical opportunities for establishing citizens’ assemblies at the local level. Wednesday, 21 October 2026 — Departure An optional informal morning session will take place before departures beginning from 11:00 AM . Participants are expected to depart on Wednesday, 21 October. Application Process Applicants must complete the official online application form before the deadline. The application requires applicants to provide information that allows the organisers to understand their background, experience and motivation. Applicants will be asked for: Name Age Country of residence Organisational affiliation A short description of their current work or engagement in democratic participation A statement explaining what they hope to gain from the workshop An explanation of how they would apply the knowledge gained in their work or community The description of current work or engagement has a maximum length of 200 words . The statement about what the applicant hopes to gain and how they will apply the learning also has a maximum length of 200 words . How to Write a Strong Application Because approximately 30 participants are expected to be selected, applicants should make their responses clear, specific and relevant. A strong application should demonstrate more than a general interest in democracy. Applicants should consider highlighting: Relevant Experience Explain your current involvement in: Youth participation Civic engagement Civil society Local government Democratic innovation Political education Community development Participatory decision-making A Concrete Idea If you already have an idea for a citizens’ assembly, explain it clearly. For example, you could describe: The issue you want citizens to deliberate on The community or municipality involved Why the issue requires citizen participation What you hope the assembly could achieve Practical Application Explain what you intend to do with the knowledge gained after returning home. This is important because the programme is intended to create practical capacity for deliberative democracy rather than simply provide theoretical knowledge. Selection Considerations The organisers expect approximately 30 participants to be selected. Geographic diversity is specifically identified as an important selection criterion. The organisers particularly encourage applications from Central and Eastern Europe . However, applicants from other Council of Europe member states can also apply, provided they meet the eligibility conditions. Important Dates Applicants should keep the following dates in mind: 10 August 2026: Call opens 7 September 2026: Application deadline 21 September 2026: Notification of results 18 October 2026: Arrival in Budapest 19–21 October 2026: Workshop 21 October 2026: Departure Applications received after 7 September 2026 will not be considered . Learn more about this opportunity HERE Where Will the Workshop Take Place? The event will be held at the: European Youth Centre Budapest Budapest, Hungary The European Youth Centre provides the setting for the Council of Europe s youth-related educational and capacity-building activities. Participants will be hosted at the centre throughout the workshop period. Why This Opportunity Matters for Young People Young people are important stakeholders in democratic decision-making, but traditional political systems do not always provide sufficient opportunities for young people to participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their communities. Deliberative democracy offers another approach by creating structured opportunities for citizens to learn about issues, hear different perspectives, discuss possible solutions and develop recommendations. For young activists and youth organisations, learning how to establish and facilitate citizens’ assemblies can therefore provide a practical tool for strengthening youth participation. The workshop can also help participants understand how youth engagement can be connected to local and regional decision-making. Final Checklist Before Applying Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should confirm that they: Are at least 18 years old Are a citizen of a Council of Europe member state Have a working level of English Are actively involved or interested in democratic participation Fit one of the target participant profiles Have a genuine interest in deliberative democracy Ideally have a concrete citizens’ assembly or deliberative-process idea Can explain how they will apply the training in their organisation or community Can attend the workshop in Budapest from 19–21 October 2026 Can arrive on 18 October 2026 Submit the online application before 7 September 2026 APPLY HERE Conclusion The Council of Europe Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies Workshop 2026 offers an excellent opportunity for eligible youth activists, civil society representatives, local and regional authorities, youth workers and democratic participation practitioners to develop practical skills in citizen engagement. Rather than focusing exclusively on theory, the workshop will teach participants how to move from the idea of a citizens’ assembly to practical planning and implementation. Participants will explore real European examples, develop their own proposals, receive expert feedback and learn how deliberative processes can be integrated into local and regional governance. The opportunity is also particularly valuable financially because selected participants will receive full coverage of travel, accommodation and meals , in accordance with Council of Europe rules. Eligible applicants should prepare their applications carefully and clearly demonstrate their current involvement in democratic participation, their motivation for attending and how they intend to use the knowledge gained in their own organisation or community.
